```{r harrell-bootstrap, cache=FALSE}
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(age_stack_diagnostics) == n_boot,
  age_stack_summary$maximum_age_raw_duplicate_id_lm == 0L,
  age_stack_summary$maximum_age_model_duplicate_id_lm == 0L,
  nrow(age_pair_count_validation) == nrow(age_score_pair_counts),
  all(age_pair_count_validation$complete_score_pairs ==
        age_pair_count_validation$successful_replicates),
  enrollment_super_replicates_retained == n_boot
)
```

```{r optimism-corrected-performance-table}
knitr::kable(
  optimism_corrected_performance[c(
    "scale", "landmark", "method", "AUC", "mean_AUC_optimism",
    "optimism_corrected_AUC", "Brier", "mean_Brier_optimism",
    "optimism_corrected_Brier", "successful_replicates",
    "failed_replicates"
  )],
  digits = 4
)
```

The failure table counts a replicate as successful only when both the
bootstrap-resample and original-cohort scores were available for that model and
landmark. This makes sparse disjoint-model failures visible in the denominator.

```{r bootstrap-failure-table}
bootstrap_failure_table <- optimism_corrected_performance[c(
  "scale", "landmark", "method", "successful_replicates", "failed_replicates"
)]
knitr::kable(bootstrap_failure_table)
```

### Age-scale bootstrap failure diagnosis

I first instrumented `r diagnostic_pilot_replicates` resamples while diagnosing
the failure path, then retained the same instrumentation for the complete
`r n_boot`-resample run reported here. The fit table is cause-specific. The
prediction table is model-specific because a death cumulative-incidence
prediction uses both the death and transplant cause-specific fits.

```{r age-bootstrap-diagnostic-tables}
zero_transplant_super_replicates <- sum(
  super_transplant_zero_by_replicate$zero_transplants_in_any_age_window
)
zero_transplant_pairs <- age_super_zero_event_link[
  age_super_zero_event_link$zero_transplants_in_any_age_window,
]
zero_transplant_pairs_all_failed <- all(
  zero_transplant_pairs$complete_score_pairs == 0L
)
zero_transplant_resample_word <- if (
  zero_transplant_super_replicates == 1L
) "resample" else "resamples"
whole_replicates_discarded <- n_boot - enrollment_super_replicates_retained
horizon_flag_has_successes <- any(
  age_horizon_summary$complete_pairs_despite_past_horizon > 0L
)
horizon_success_phrase <- if (horizon_flag_has_successes) {
  "did occur"
} else "did not occur"
age_failure_classification <- if (
  zero_transplant_super_replicates > 0L &&
    zero_transplant_pairs_all_failed &&
    whole_replicates_discarded == 0L
) {
  "genuine sparse competing-event fits, not an ID or whole-replicate control-flow bug"
} else {
  "not resolved by the recorded diagnostics"
}

knitr::kable(age_stack_summary)
knitr::kable(age_fit_failure_tally)
knitr::kable(age_prediction_failure_tally)
knitr::kable(age_failure_reason_tally)
knitr::kable(age_super_zero_event_link)
knitr::kable(age_horizon_summary)
```

All resampled subject copies had distinct analysis identifiers, and the maximum
duplicate count for `(id, LM)` was
`r age_stack_summary$maximum_age_model_duplicate_id_lm`. There were
`r age_stack_summary$stack_build_errors` stack-build errors and
`r age_stack_summary$unexpected_replicate_errors` unexpected replicate errors.
The enrollment supermodel retained complete pairs from all `r n_boot`
resamples, so the safety wrapper discarded `r whole_replicates_discarded` whole
replicates when an age component failed.

The dominant mechanism was sparse transplantation. In
`r zero_transplant_super_replicates` `r zero_transplant_resample_word`, at least
one age window had no transplants. Every such resample lacked a complete
age-supermodel score pair at
every age landmark. The cause-specific table shows the associated convergence
warnings and non-finite transplant-model coefficients. Because the age
supermodel uses one competing-risk fit across all landmarks, an undefined
transplant linear predictor prevents the death cumulative-incidence prediction
at every landmark; this is why the supermodel success counts were nearly
uniform. Scoring remained landmark-specific and did not discard the other age
landmarks when only a score calculation failed.

The horizon check did not explain the failures. Complete score pairs
`r horizon_success_phrase` in rows whose horizon passed the last observed event,
consistent with the step-function baseline hazard carrying forward after that
event. I therefore classified the failure as `r age_failure_classification`.

I did not alter the age model or replace failed replicates. The optimism-corrected
age values are conditional on the subset of resamples with finite competing-risk
fits and complete train/test scores, so I would not use them as primary
performance estimates. A future analysis could evaluate a denser age grid, a
simpler transplant model, or a prespecified penalized competing-risk fit, but
each would change the model and requires its own validation.

On the current attained-age grid, each landmark already has its own baseline
because the windows do not overlap. With `r length(age_landmarks)` landmarks
and a quadratic laboratory basis containing `r length(age_basis) + 1L`
coefficients per laboratory, the laboratory effects are also effectively
saturated across those landmarks. The primary attained-age supermodel therefore
pools only male sex, disease stage, and treatment across landmarks; it cannot
show the smoothing advantage that would require a denser, overlapping grid.

# Calibration

The apparent calibration plots rendered at every requested landmark. I used
the same quantile grouping on both scales and retained the condition table so a
future failure will be visible rather than silently dropped.

```{r enrollment-calibration, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
old_parameters <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
enrollment_calibration_arguments <- list(
  object = list("Enrollment scale" = enrollment_predictions),
  times = enrollment_landmarks,
  id_col = "id",
  cause = cause_of_interest,
  method = "quantile",
  q = 4,
  legend = FALSE,
  xlim = c(0, 1),
  ylim = c(0, 1)
)
enrollment_calibration_record <- capture_conditions(do.call(
  calplot,
  enrollment_calibration_arguments
))
par(old_parameters)

if (inherits(enrollment_calibration_record$value, "error")) {
  stop(
    "Enrollment calibration failed: ",
    conditionMessage(enrollment_calibration_record$value)
  )
}
```

```{r age-calibration, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
old_parameters <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
age_calibration_arguments <- list(
  object = list("Age scale" = age_predictions),
  times = age_landmarks,
  id_col = "id",
  cause = cause_of_interest,
  method = "quantile",
  q = 4,
  legend = FALSE,
  xlim = c(0, 1),
  ylim = c(0, 1)
)
age_calibration_record <- capture_conditions(do.call(
  calplot,
  age_calibration_arguments
))
par(old_parameters)

if (inherits(age_calibration_record$value, "error")) {
  stop(
    "Age calibration failed: ",
    conditionMessage(age_calibration_record$value)
  )
}
```

```{r calibration-conditions}
calibration_conditions <- data.frame(
  scale = c("Enrollment time", "Attained age"),
  warning_count = c(
    length(enrollment_calibration_record$warnings),
    length(age_calibration_record$warnings)
  ),
  error = c(
    if (inherits(enrollment_calibration_record$value, "error")) conditionMessage(enrollment_calibration_record$value) else "",
    if (inherits(age_calibration_record$value, "error")) conditionMessage(age_calibration_record$value) else ""
  ),
  row.names = NULL
)

knitr::kable(calibration_conditions)
```

# Interpretation

The enrollment analysis used a common origin and updated attained age as a
predictor. The attained-age analysis used age as the clock, excluded age from
the right-hand side, and enforced observation by each landmark. The substantive
non-age covariates and the two laboratory interaction structures were identical.
The enrollment supermodel additionally included estimable centered LM main
effects. The primary attained-age supermodel did not: its non-overlapping
windows made LM constant within every event risk set, and the demonstration fit
returned non-estimable LM coefficients.

The age-scale risk-set pattern illustrated the practical difference: people
could enter as age advanced, so a later age landmark could contain more eligible
subjects than an earlier one. Strict entry made that membership rule explicit.

The disjoint fits showed the cost of spending a full coefficient vector at each
landmark. I retained every warning and non-estimable coefficient in the output,
and I left unavailable predictions missing rather than changing a sparse model.
The bootstrap likewise reports the number of complete resample-and-test pairs
for every model and landmark, so the corrected performance estimates can be
read together with their failure counts.

The bootstrap diagnosis traced the low attained-age completion rate to sparse
transplant fits, not duplicated bootstrap identifiers or whole-replicate loss.
Because the death cumulative incidence depends on the transplant hazard, a
non-finite transplant fit invalidated predictions from the shared age
supermodel. I therefore treated the corrected attained-age performance as
conditional and exploratory rather than as a primary estimate.

This attained-age comparison cannot demonstrate smoothing of the laboratory
effects. Its disjoint windows give each landmark a separate baseline, and its
quadratic laboratory basis is effectively saturated over the observed age
landmarks. On this grid, the attained-age supermodel pools male sex, disease
stage, and treatment; a denser overlapping grid would be needed to study the
additional pooling available from an LM main effect and smoother laboratory
trajectories.

Within-window delayed entry was not part of this primary comparison. In the
separate NAFLD application, it added very little analyzable longitudinal
information because most later entrants lacked a laboratory value at their
analysis entry. That finding supports treating strict entry as the clearer
primary analysis rather than assuming delayed entry will automatically recover
substantial usable data.
